headline: VidTube Channel That Reviews 'Different Types of Silence' Hits 1 Million Subscribers
subheadline: Creator has catalogued 847 distinct silence varieties; fans debate favorites
summary: A VidTube channel dedicated entirely to reviewing and rating silence has developed a devoted following.
content:
VidTube creator @SilenceReviewer has reached 1 million subscribers with a channel devoted entirely to reviewing different types of silence—and the community has strong opinions.

"Today we're reviewing the silence after someone says something they shouldn't have at dinner," begins a typical video, which then features 10 minutes of @SilenceReviewer sitting quietly, occasionally nodding, before delivering a verdict: "Tension: 9/10. Awkwardness: 8/10. Probability someone fake-coughs to break it: High. Overall: A classic silence. Recommended."

The channel has catalogued 847 distinct varieties of silence, from "elevator silence between two people who almost dated" to "the silence when everyone realizes the 'mute' button wasn't on."

"I thought it was a joke when I started," said @SilenceReviewer in a rare interview conducted, appropriately, mostly in silence. "But then I realized silence is the most underappreciated sound. People don't pay attention to it. They should."

The community has developed sophisticated terminology. "Weight" refers to how heavy a silence feels. "Echo potential" describes whether the silence makes you replay what preceded it. "Exit difficulty" rates how hard it is to end the silence naturally.

Fan favorites include "silence in a library when someone's phone goes off" (praised for its "collective psychic pressure") and "silence after you wave at someone who wasn't waving at you" (described as "brutally immersive").

The most controversial review was "the silence of space," which some fans argued was "cheating" while others called it "the purest form."

"That's not reviewable silence," commented one user. "That's just absence. Real silence requires the possibility of sound."

The debate thread has 847 comments and counting. Appropriately, many are blank.
author: Chris Patterson, Digital Culture
